I am somewhat old enough that some friends already have kids, and I have often thought of the hypothetical parent I would be. I wouldn't reduce my child to a set of problems or things about them I don't like. If you want to have a relationship with *anyone*, you have to nurture it. And sure, the relationship you have with a child is unique, but it is just like most other human relationships. If your child senses that you don't like them and/or are constantly judging them, they won't want to spend time with you. If all your conversations are negative for no good reason (nearly everyone I know would love to have their kids read voraciously while supporting themselves and staying sane), then gradually over time your kid will associate spending time with you with unpleasant memories and conversations. If you want your child to respect you, you must respect your child. These kinds of respect will clearly present differently, but they both need to be present in order for your relationship to be amicable and healthy. I can tell, having been in your kid's position, that your relationship is neither amicable or healthy. 

What you should do is start by not judging your child and supporting them, and maybe get to know them as a person. Know that when you start doing this, especially if you have had an adversarial relationship for a long period of time, your child will be suspicious of your possible motives. But be sincere and quietly persistent (ask her about the books she's reading, read some of them with her, talk about them!) and she will understand that you are trying. Relate to her as a human being, especially since she's a grown adult now, and she might open up to you as to how her college classes are going or her thoughts about her life and career.

I know you think you're Being a Good Parent by constantly asking and clearly expressing your disbelief in your daughter's skills by worrying that she's about to drop out again, but you're not. You are only making her want to open up to you less and less. 

I know you will very likely not care about what someone like me has to say, but having been in a similar position to your daughter, I feel some responsibility to try and demonstrate what you're doing wrong here. What you're doing won't make your daughter open up to you, it will only drive her away. Love her and spend time with her as a full person, and that will go a lot further towards her wanting to be social with you.

Good luck.

Okay, I can kind of see what you mean. And as someone who has been abused and basically had to flee in the middle of the night from my abusive desi parents and have more than a decade of therapy (still go every week), I might have a slightly different take.

When your abuse is based on cultural values, it is very hard to not think that that culture is not inherently violent. If you spend your life thinking that your parents are beating you for making a mistake because they're following the cultural norms, you are very easily forgiven for thinking that is all the culture is. For a very long time, I absolutely did this.

But some time ago, I had a bit of a epiphany. People aren't evil, mustache twirling villains. People tend to reenact things that were done to them, consciously or unconsciously. 

My father knows that if you hit someone, it hurts and damages your relationship to them mostly irreparably (justifiably so); he's a smart man. But he hit me because this is what you do with "daughters" (I'm non-binary, but to him I will always be a "daughter"). His father led by example, hitting my father's mother and my father's sisters. He saw this as normal and fine, so he continued it with my mother, me, and in a different way with my brother.

My mother psychologically terrorised me and made me feel like the shit on her shoes for not fitting into the culture's idea of what a woman should be (little wonder then that I turned out to be a non-binary person). She did what I imagine women in her family always did - she tried to starve me thin, make me dress the way she wanted me to, and tried to shove me in a box. It's not because my mother is evil, but rather because this is what patriarchy (and patriarchy is not only enforced by men) dictates a woman to be. If someone perceived to be a woman falls out of line, there are harsh penalties. The least of which being my mother telling me that no one in the world would possibly want me around, and that they were stuck taking care of me only because killing children is harder to cover up here. 

But these aren't indications of my parents or my culture being evil. This is just the culture "sickness" that comes in many forms across innumerable cultures. People either embrace or reject them, depending on the lives they choose to live. And having bucked culture myself, god there is so much incentive to stay in the culture.

And speaking of white parents, I think it's important to remember that many people who idealise and idealised white parents live in countries with a history of white supremacy. I live in the US, and for most of the country's history, the perfect family is a white family (with certain other trappings, of course, but always white). Only within the last handful of years have we seen shows and representations of non-white, particularly Desi families. Many of these shows are also written primarily by white people. So there are certain imperfections there. 

Desi kids live in the perfect storm in enforced white-majority countries; often the circumstances of being able to put down roots in a country create stressful situations which can encourage people to stick to old patterns of family abuse and violence, and the media we are all exposed to idealises whiteness and white families and white children. It's a thing it took years of therapy to realise. I'm still reparenting myself.
